articles.title_orig: Dialogue can help prevent differences from destabilizing overall Sino-US economic ties: China Daily editorial
articles.title_zh: Dialogue can help prevent differences from destabilizing overall Sino-US economic ties: China Daily editorial
articles.content_orig:
chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-15 20:03
The political storm surrounding Nvidia soon after the midterm elections in the United States is about considerably more than a company or the conduct of its former chief executive. Its timing, the congressional reaction and the legislative ambitions now gathering momentum in Washington point to a larger objective: building political support for tougher high-tech restrictions against China.
The speed with which a corporate controversy has been converted into an argument for sweeping technology restrictions is revealing. The objective is to make commercial engagement with China in high-tech sectors politically indefensible.
The timing of the congressional questioning is equally suggestive. Its proximity to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, where artificial intelligence is expected to feature prominently in discussions, is difficult to dismiss as coincidence. While the APEC meeting offers an opportunity to explore practical cooperation and establish channels for AI dialogue, the political theater of the US Congress bodes otherwise.
The US administration's own rhetoric also illustrates its intention. Its promotion of "Pax Silica", an initiative designed to make AI and semiconductor supply chains less dependent on China, seeks to turn technological competition into a geopolitical alignment test for other countries. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's latest attempt to baselessly link Chinese AI models to cyberattacks that disrupted supermarket refrigeration systems in France is another example. Turning an unresolved cybersecurity incident into an "indictment" of another country's technology says more about the political anxieties of some in Washington than about the actual risks of AI.
Some US officials repeatedly invoke "security" to justify restricting Chinese technology, while the US itself continues to face its own serious AI-related cybersecurity and governance challenges. The true concern driving Washington's restrictions against Chinese AI is the vitality and competitiveness of China's AI industry. Labeling Chinese models as "dangerous", without credible evidence, is easier than explaining why US companies need to be protected from competition through political intervention rather than outperforming their competitors through innovation.
As Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning stressed, Beijing opposes the abuse of export controls, which disrupts the stability of the global industry and supply chains and serves nobody's interests.
Notably though, the channels between the two countries are continuing to produce tangible results, despite the noise from Washington. On Friday, the two sides held the first meeting of the trade council under the China-US economic and trade consultation mechanism. The video meeting featured candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on tariffs, reciprocal tariff reductions covering approximately $30 billion worth of goods, agricultural trade and other issues of mutual concern.
The two sides pledged to strengthen communication, resolve their respective economic and trade concerns, expand cooperation and shorten the list of outstanding issues. The meeting shows that, despite their differences, the world's two largest economies can identify shared interests, negotiate workable arrangements and prevent differences from overwhelming the broader economic ties.
A similar message emerged from Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi's meeting on Friday with US representatives attending the US-China Political Dialogue 2026 in Beijing. Wang called on both sides to clarify the goals of their joint efforts, expand mutually beneficial cooperation and consolidate the foundations of bilateral relations. Mutual respect, peaceful coexistence and win-win cooperation, Wang emphasized, should guide efforts to implement the consensus of the two heads of state on building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.
AI should be an important part of this agenda, not its casualty. Differences over data governance, cybersecurity and technology standards deserve serious discussion. Unfoundedly assigning national labels of "danger" to AI models only politicizes technical questions and makes meaningful cooperation harder.
The imperative task is to preserve the diplomatic space in which the differences between China and the US in AI and other sectors can be managed and common interests advanced.
To that end, the two sides should work together to lengthen the list of cooperation, and shorten the list of issues. China and the US have the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people.

articles.title_orig: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
One of the camps in Al-Mawasi in southern Gaza
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.
Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.
A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".
Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.
The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.
Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".
It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."
Al-Qassam Brigades wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions", and was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".
It described his killing as a "cowardly assassination".
Younis, 53, had been in his position since 15 September, following the death of the brigade's previous commander, Nael Abu Obeid.
He joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and held several senior operational roles before becoming commander. His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.
The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed an 251 others taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Palestinian territory, the health ministry there says.
Though a ceasefire was reached last October, Israel has continued strikes it says are targeting remaining Hamas militants, which it argues it has the right to do under the terms of the ceasefire agreement.
More than 1,640 people have been killed in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Update November 15: An earlier version of this article referred to Israel carrying out 'occasional' strikes in Gaza following a ceasefire in October 2025. This word has been removed to better reflect the frequency of Israeli strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire.

articles.title_orig: Consumer Alert: Urgent Park Outside Recall Issued for Nearly 721K BMW Vehicles - NHTSA | National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (.gov)
articles.title_zh: Consumer Alert: Urgent Park Outside Recall Issued for Nearly 721K BMW Vehicles - NHTSA | National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (.gov)
articles.source: NHTSA | National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (.gov)
articles.content_orig:
The new recall covers 2012-2018 BMW 3 Series, 5 Series, X1, X3, X4 and Z4 models, and BMW is still developing the repair.
Owners of 720,796 BMWs are being told to park outside, away from buildings and other vehicles, because a water pump connector BMW already recalled in 2024 can still short circuit and start a fire while the car is parked and switched off. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced the new recall on Friday, and BMW doesn’t have a repair for it yet.
These are the same cars that went through the first water pump recall, mostly four-cylinder 3 Series, 5 Series, X1, X3 and X4 models built between 2012 and 2018. BMW knows of about 10 incidents in the US that are or may be linked to the defect, and all of them happened in cars that had already received the 2024 fix. No crashes or injuries have been reported.
NHTSA’s consumer alert lists recall 26V-733 for these models:
NHTSA names whole model lines this time, but the 2024 recall was more specific: the 228i, 328i and 428i and their xDrive versions, the 528i, the X1, X3 and X4 28i models, the Z4 sDrive28i and the X5 xDrive40e plug-in hybrid. All of them use BMW’s N20 or N26 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder. If your car wears one of those badges, assume it’s affected until the VIN lookup says otherwise.
The first recall, 24V-608, blamed blow-by liquid from the crankcase ventilation system, which could collect on the intake air hose and drip onto the electric water pump’s plug connector. Dealers inspected the pump and connector, replaced them if they were damaged, and fitted a splash shield over the connector to keep future drips off.
BMW’s new filing points to the connector itself. The material can degrade and let moisture into the pump, and BMW’s testing found embrittlement and cracks in the connectors. A splash shield can’t do much about plastic that’s cracking underneath it. After its review found more overheating cases in cars that had already been repaired, BMW decided on Oct. 28 to recall them again.
Park outside, away from your house, your garage and other cars. That applies even if your car already had the 2024 repair, because NHTSA says previously repaired vehicles will need the new remedy too. BMW will start mailing owner letters on Dec. 25, 2026 , and VINs and license plates become searchable on NHTSA.gov/Recalls the same day. Until then, BMW’s recall hotline is 800-525-7417, and NHTSA’s Vehicle Safety Hotline is 888-327-4236. The repair will be free at BMW dealers once it exists, but BMW hasn’t said what it involves or when parts will be ready.

articles.title_orig: Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia?
articles.title_zh: Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia?
articles.content_orig:
The United States has pitched a new pathway for Ukraine to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), an aspiration that Kyiv has long held as a means to guarantee its defence against Russia, almost five years into their war.
But the administration of President Donald Trump has suggested that Ukraine would need to agree to give up all of the Donbas region in the country’s east, which Russian President Vladimir Putin has demanded as one of his conditions for ending the war.
The idea, according to Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, was communicated to him by Trump’s negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the latest round of US-mediated peace talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week.
After the Abu Dhabi round of talks, Kushner and Witkoff met Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then briefed Zelenskyy in Dublin, before a meeting of European leaders in the Irish capital on Friday.
Ukraine applied to become a member of NATO in September 2022, seeking to fortify its borders with Russia.
But the Kremlin has repeatedly said Ukraine becoming a member of NATO would demand “a harsh response” from Russia.
So will Washington’s latest pitch be acceptable to both Ukraine and Russia?
On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that Kushner and Witkoff had suggested that Ukraine could become a NATO member if it ceded control of Donbas in the east.
He said, “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'”
“NATO is back on the agenda” since it is part of an “extremely difficult” conversation between Ukraine and Russia which would determine the future of European security, Zelenskyy said.
Putin has been against Ukraine’s NATO membership and has demanded that the alliance pull back its troops from countries bordering Russia.
“This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.
“Real security in Europe means the EU [European Union] and NATO. That’s it. There is no other security in Europe.”
Ian Lesser, distinguished fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States told Al Jazeera that the US proposal, if accurate, is significant because it articulates very directly an approach long current in US administration circles that Ukraine should be prepared to make territorial concessions in the service of a settlement.
“The NATO element seems very doubtful. Surely attractive to Ukraine, but [it is] hard to imagine Moscow agreeing to this. And some NATO members will be doubtful too,” he said.
Chris Featherstone, a political scientist from the University of York in the United Kingdom argued that the proposal was a major departure from previously held positions.
“The US has been very cautious about getting further involved in Ukraine, with the Biden administration giving military support, but clearly opposing any ideas of Western involvement on the ground. Trump has seemed to be very sympathetic to the Russian cause, and has had significant blow ups with Zelensky, so this proposal is certainly a surprise,” he noted.
He told Al Jazeera that offering NATO membership in a peace settlement would give significant support to Ukraine should Russia reinitiate the conflict in the future.
“In the light of Trump’s repeated attacks on NATO this could be seen as a recommitment to the alliance. However there would be questions over whether Trump could bring other NATO allies to support the proposal,” he added.
Ukraine applied to become a NATO member in September 2022, just months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the country.
Since then, Zelenskyy, his officials and Ukrainians around the world have been lobbying NATO nations to speed up Kyiv’s accession process.
But NATO members remain divided over offering Ukraine alliance membership amid an ongoing war despite a broad consensus to signal strong support for Kyiv.
NATO members bordering Russia, like Lithuania and Poland, have been most enthusiastic about backing Ukraine’s ambitions. Several other nations in the alliance have also been supportive of an expedited process for Kyiv to join, amid concerns about corruption in Ukraine and while seeking an end to the war with Russia as a condition for the country to become a NATO member.
But under President Trump, the US has been far less receptive to Ukraine’s calls for NATO membership. Trump has publicly told Ukraine to give up on hopes of joining the alliance.
Yet, while the new proposal from Witkoff and Kushner revives Ukraine’s hopes of joining NATO, it demands a compromise that no government in Kyiv can easily make.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that the prospect of Ukraine joining NATO in exchange for ceding territory had not been raised by members of the alliance before and reiterated that Kyiv would not give up any of its territories.
But he said if Ukraine received a peace deal which included security guarantees, the right to maintain a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild the country, then he would hold a national referendum on the question of ceding territory in exchange for NATO membership.
Featherstone noted that Ukraine has been fighting for a long time, and has consistently maintained that it will not relinquish it’s territory in a peace deal.
“The proposal from the Trump administration is clearly an attempt to test this Ukrainian position, in an effort to confront the impasse,” he said.
“NATO membership would give a level of security that Ukraine would likely welcome, however, this would be a big sacrifice of territory and sovereignty. After years of Trump’s questioning of the NATO commitment, Ukraine would need a strong statement of commitment to its defence should they be considering any proposal like this,” he added.
The Kremlin has not yet responded to the latest US proposal.
But it has maintained a strict position that Ukraine’s NATO membership is a red line for Moscow and a direct threat to Russia’s national security. In fact, Putin has also cited the issue of Ukraine’s NATO aspirations as one reason why Russia launched its war in 2022.
Despite Kushner and Witkoff’s meetings with Putin, the Kremlin has shown little appetite for a change in that position. Moscow has continued, throughout the war, to demand that Ukraine abandon its NATO ambitions and maintain a neutral and demilitarised status. Russia has also firmly opposed any deployment of Western troops or peacekeepers on Ukrainian soil.
In addition to demanding that Ukraine give up its NATO dreams, Moscow has also insisted that Ukraine should cede sovereignty over the Donbas region, in addition to parts of Zaporizhia and Kherson provinces that Russia already occupies.
Just as the new US proposal asks Ukraine to give up some territory in return for a NATO seat, it offers Russia a bargain — withdraw the red line on Ukraine’s NATO membership and get Donbas in exchange.
The region in eastern Ukraine has historically been the country’s industrial heartland and is therefore a critical economic engine.
A majority of people in the Donbas identify as ethnically Ukrainian, but a minority identifies as ethnically Russian. The Russian language is also widely spoken in the region — a legacy of Russian migration there in the 19th century and then under the Soviet Union.
Russia accuses Ukraine of discriminating against Russian-speaking and ethnically Russian people in the Donbas, and has used this claim to justify its demand that Kyiv hand over the region to Moscow.
The region consists of the provinces of Luhansk and Donetsk. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has occupied almost all of Luhansk and most of Donetsk. In all, it controls about 88 percent of the Donbas region. But it has consistently demanded that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the remaining parts of the Donbas they currently hold.

articles.title_orig: US, China, Russia plan unprecedented meeting at APEC
articles.title_zh: US, China, Russia plan unprecedented meeting at APEC
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

articles.title_orig: How Jensen Huang Built the Backdoor Route That Keeps Beijing in the AI Race
articles.title_zh: How Jensen Huang Built the Backdoor Route That Keeps Beijing in the AI Race
articles.content_orig:
Headquartered in a curved glass skyscraper that boasts commanding views over Singapore’s Marina Bay district, Megaspeed International is just the type of fast-growing tech start-up that Asia’s wealthy city-state has been keen to attract.
In three years, the corporate entity has gone from an inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US.
But its rapid rise has also propelled it to the center of an alleged spy scandal that’s now engulfing Nvidia , the $4 trillion company behind the world’s most advanced chips.
At the same time, suspicions that Megaspeed may be exploiting a loophole in US export controls is exacerbating a rift within the US government on how to best keep China from accessing its most sensitive technologies.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to having an affair. Congress has also called on him to testify behind closed doors about his romantic relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, whom US officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Beijing has said the claim is a “groundless” attempt to smear China.
Also known as Huang Le , the 43-year-old Chinese executive played an integral role in establishing Megaspeed, according to corporate documents and media reports. CNN has made continued efforts to reach her for comment.
But as Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia, it came under the scrutiny of the Singaporean government, as well as US officials concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers.
“Chips are the absolute ground-zero of all other technology,” said Alex Capri, a senior lecturer in the business school at the National University of Singapore. “The appetite for Nvidia’s chips in China is absolutely insatiable… Nvidia chips are still far and away the best.”
But US export controls have fettered Chinese access to its most advanced semiconductor technology, spawning a shadow industry of complex transactions, shell companies and chip smuggling – of which Megaspeed is now under suspicion by US authorities and lawmakers of helping enable.
Nvidia’s CEO is out after 33 years. What’s next?
On Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong said in a statement the company has cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce and has retained a US law firm to independently verify its compliance with export controls.
“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously. Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government,” the statement said.
In a new statement on Sunday, Megaspeed said that Huang left the company on August 30, 2025, and currently holds no role there.
“Megaspeed is aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence,” the statement said.
In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia’s most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China’s tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.
US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those.
Incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, the company’s name changed to Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became a director through November of that year. Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia.
Capri, who also wrote the book, “Techno-Nationalism: How It’s Reshaping Trade, Geopolitics and Society,” said Megaspeed’s business model, in which it builds data centers and rents out its computing services, gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips.
“If you put me on the restricted list to drive a Ferrari, and I say ‘Okay, well I can’t buy a Ferrari, I can’t import a Ferrari, but I can just go to a car dealership and rent a Ferrari,’ right? And do whatever I want with the Ferrari,” he said. “That’s an issue. It’s the car dealership that you have to control.”
Corporate filings show connections between subsidiary entities of Megaspeed and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, including the pledging of collateral. CNN has sought comment from Alibaba.
In other cases, Chinese buyers have been able to procure sensitive components of their own, often done through a web of ghost corporations and brokers through which the chips – sometimes concealed in other electronics or containers – can reach end users in China, experts said.
Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year.
“This is a pipeline that has developed that benefits from the fact that there is minimal scrutiny on US air data, that you can bring things into Singapore, Malaysia, Central and Southeast Asia and then move those goods, sometimes through Thailand, into China,” trade data investigator William George told CNN.
“It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks,” he said.
Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company’s server purchases and their final destinations.
In a statement, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence Huang that had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information “to downplay her role” at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.
The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws.
A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.
Jensen Huang, who has accompanied US President Donald Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, has lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue.
However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well.
They include Northwestern Polytechnical University, based in Xi’an, the capital of China’s Shaanxi province, one of the nation’s leading universities with military ties, known collectively as the “Seven Sons of National Defense.”
Northwestern Polytechnical University has been on the US Department of Commerce’s Entity List since 2001, yet it bought four H200 chips last month for $250,000, according to procurement records published on its own website that have since been deleted.
Northwestern Polytechnical University did not respond to a phone call from CNN seeking comment.
Despite investigation by the US, Megaspeed has not been labeled a national security threat or subject to limitations on chip purchases — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that led to a confrontation by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers, whose party recently won control of the House and Senate, are calling for greater oversight for US exports of advanced chips, days before Trump’s due to meet Xi for the third time this year in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

articles.title_orig: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base
articles.title_zh: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base
articles.content_orig:
A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries he suffered when a grass fire swept through a military training area last month.
Four people were killed initially and dozens were injured when the fire, which ignited during a live fire training exercise, spread rapidly through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright carried by strong winds on 17 October.
Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco, who had been receiving medical care in Ontario, died on Friday, the Canadian Armed Forces said in a statement.
Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X: "Canadians are holding Private Dal Bianco's loved ones, and all those still grieving in the wake of this terrible tragedy, in our hearts."
The Canadian Armed Forces said that 24 military personnel were still in hospital receiving treatment, while 14 had been released as of Saturday. Thirty-eight military personnel had been injured in total.
Members of 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group had been conducting live-fire training at the base, in the province of Alberta, when the fire broke out.
Military officials said at the time that the fire spread across a kilometre in a matter of seconds, taking many of those on the base by surprise.
Firefighters battled the blaze through the night, while nearby hospitals became inundated by injured personnel and staff.
Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".
An investigation found that the fire was likely sparked by a grenade launcher being fired on the base's grenade range, officials said.
Firefighters on the base had known about the fire but could not tackle it because it was in a danger area that could contain unspent explosives.
Canadian Chief of the Defence Staff Gen Jennie Carignan said the nation's armed forces were "heartbroken" by the loss of Dal Bianco, while Defence Minister David McGuinty offered his "deepest condolences" to his family, friends and colleagues.
"No words can ease the pain of losing a loved one, and my thoughts remain with all those affected by this tragedy," he said.
"We remain committed to supporting the families and the Canadian Armed Forces community during this profoundly difficult time, and to honouring Private Dal Bianco's service, dedication and sacrifice to Canada."

articles.title_orig: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe into reports about its business
articles.title_zh: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe into reports about its business
articles.content_orig:
Megaspeed told CNBC Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and said it has launched an internal probe into media reports concerning its business and supply chain.
The Singapore-based cloud computing company has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times.
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12 amid fallout from reports about his extramarital relationships, one of which was reportedly a direct report.
"Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Company," Megaspeed said in an emailed statement shared with CNBC. "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," it added.
Megaspeed describes itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the region, allowing customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs, or graphics processing units — specialized chips designed to do many calculations at the same time.
The company, which has offices in Singapore and Indonesia, has previously faced media and government scrutiny over whether chips supplied through its business were redirected to customers in China.
Megaspeed said Sunday that media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations are not supported by verifiable evidence and it has retained external legal counsel to conduct a "thorough internal investigation."
"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.
The company added that it will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate.

articles.content_orig:

Donald Trump will meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China next week for an unprecedented three-way meeting between the leaders of the US , Russia , and China, with nuclear weapons and the war in Iran expected to be on the agenda.
The meeting will take place on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the White House confirmed on Friday. It will bring together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, although all three have held bilateral talks with one another.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting comes nine months after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.
The treaty, which expired in February, had placed limits on the two countries’ strategic nuclear arsenals, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without those restrictions for the first time in more than half a century.
Mr Trump has rejected Russia's offer to extend it for another year, saying he wanted a new agreement that would also include China.
Beijing has resisted joining such negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow. China has more than 600 nuclear warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each for Russia and the US.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told reporters, according to Reuters. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think ​it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations about adult things.”
Mr Trump also intends to discuss the war in Iran with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, but Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not expected to feature, the official said. “We’ve had many meetings ⁠recently with ​the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, ​so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that his country must be involved in any discussions about its future.
Russia had previously proposed the three-way meeting, with Mr Putin reportedly keen to use it to discuss Ukraine. The Russian president had floated the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump last month, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had warned against giving Putin such a platform. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” he said last month, adding that it would only “encourage Putin to continue this war”.
The planned summit has also drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar settlement in Europe. The prospect of Mr Trump, Mr Putin, and Mr Xi meeting without Ukraine has revived concerns about major powers making decisions that affect other countries without consulting them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparison, saying that any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries. He nevertheless described a meeting between the three leaders as “extremely significant”. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Mr Trump is due to visit Manila on Tuesday for talks with leaders of the Association of South-east Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with Xi on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral meeting.
The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.

articles.title_orig: Russell Brand: Alleged rape victim wants age of consent law changed
articles.title_zh: Russell Brand: Alleged rape victim wants age of consent law changed
articles.content_orig:
A woman who alleges that she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity and is campaigning for a staggered age of consent in an interview with the Sunday Times.
Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. She was known under the pseudonym 'Alice'. Brand denied the allegations at the time.
None of the women in the 2023 media investigation were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.
Reacting to the proposal, Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh said it would be a "massive step" to change the age of consent law, but that it "deserves proper consideration and scrutiny".
Speaking to the Sunday Times, she added that it was "disgusting" that a culture existed in the 2000s that "normalised and celebrated" celebrities having relationships with teenagers.
On Monday the entertainer was sentenced to 10 and a half years for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.
The Sunday Times reported that Latter had initially described the allegation about Brand to them as a sexual assault and that is how they reported it in their 2023 investigation.
Latter, 37, "now calls this allegation rape", the paper said.
Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time, when she was on her way home from a shopping trip. She said Brand was working at MTV.
She told the paper: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power]."
She said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.
It was towards the end of their relationship that Latter was allegedly orally raped by Brand, according to the Sunday Times.
Latter said that she was now campaigning for the introduction of a "staggered" age of consent that would prohibit relationships between 16- and 17-year-olds and adults.
"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other," she told the paper. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."
She also told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.
In her interview with the Sunday Times she said that the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but the police wanted her to be part of a "subsequent trial".
A Met Police spokesperson said: "Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.
"Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.
"This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."
A spokesperson for the Crown Prosecution Service said it would "continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible".

articles.title_orig: What can be done about the A120's dead deer problem?
articles.title_zh: What can be done about the A120's dead deer problem?
articles.content_orig:
The number of deer lying dead along the A120 has been a hot topic in a corner of Essex recently.
People living near Great Dunmow believe the problem is getting worse, and figures from Uttlesford District Council back them up.
So what can be done to improve the situation?
On a two-mile (about 3km) stretch of the A120 near Great Dunmow, Sam Mannock counts 15 dead deer lying by the road.
"It's not only deer," she explains. "There was even a large white owl lying at the side of the road."
Mannock is not wrong in thinking the number of carcasses is higher than usual.
Figures from the district council show 43 reports of dead deer and muntjac have been made so far in 2026.
That is more than the 39 reports in the whole of 2025 and 42 the year before.
"Seeing all these animals just littered at the side of the road is so upsetting, it's so awful to see," she says.
"There are children going backwards and forwards and they're going to start to think that is normal and that is the way things should be."
The issue has become a hot topic on local Facebook groups. Some point the finger at developers for building over green spaces.
A council spokeswoman suggests the autumn rutting season could also be to blame, as deer movement increases.
Although the exact numbers are unknown, it is estimated the number of deer killed or injured on UK roads every year exceeds 40,000.
The British Deer Society's Charles Smith-Jones says driver vigilance can help get these numbers down.
"We've all seen the wildlife signs on the roads with the running deer image on it, but we just get used to them – we blank them as we travel along our regular routes," he says.
It all depends on what road an animal is killed on and which part of it the body lies.
On major routes such as the M25, the A12 and the A120, National Highways is responsible for removing dead animals which are on the carriageway or central reservation.
If the animal is on a smaller route or the verge on an A-road, the local council is responsible
"While reports are spread across the district rather than concentrated in the Great Dunmow area, the figures suggest there may be a slight increase this year," a spokesman for Uttlesford District Council says.
"The figures should be treated as indicative, as some carcasses are removed by council crews during routine work without a formal report being recorded."
A National Highways spokesman says dead animals are removed if they pose a safety risk to motorists.
Deer populations can rise quickly as they do not have any natural predators, but this can lead to woodlands being damaged and accidents on the road.
Culls take place annually in the UK, usually running through the winter.
Mannock believes a more humane approach of using appropriate fencing could also mitigate the issue.
"Fences maybe aren't being looked after and maintained [which allows] these beautiful animals to just keep running on to roads," she says.
"The landscapes they once had and lived on are now disappearing."
Another suggestion is for people to eat more venison , creating a supply chain for it.
People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals has also proposed habitat modification and limiting access to artificial food sources as potential solutions.
The exact number of wild deer in the UK is not known, but the government estimates there are about two million.

articles.title_orig: Turkish husband, who pushed pregnant wife off cliff, released from prison 6 years into life sentence
articles.title_zh: Turkish husband, who pushed pregnant wife off cliff, released from prison 6 years into life sentence
articles.content_orig:
A Turkish man sentenced to life in prison for pushing his pregnant wife to her death off a famed 1,000-foot cliff for a life insurance policy payout was set free after only six years, sparking intense backlash.
Hakan Aysal was freed from a high-security prison as Turkey’s Supreme Court’s Criminal General Assembly reviews an appeal on the convicted killer’s lifetime sentence for the 2018 death of his wife, Semra Aysal, Turkish newspaper Cumhuriyet reported Friday.
“My client’s six years of unjust imprisonment, approximately four of which he spent in solitary confinement, has come to an end,” Aysal’s lawyer said, according to the outlet.
Aysal, 45, was serving an aggravated life imprisonment sentence for the premeditated killing of his 32-year-old wife, whom he shoved off the scenic Butterfly Valley cliff after taking selfies together.
Aysal was convicted in October 2022.
Aysal’s lawyers and Supreme Court Chief Prosecutor Ömer Taş claimed there was a lack of sufficient, convincing evidence to convict the killer husband.
Turkish prosecutors had argued that Aysal shoved his wife, who was seven months pregnant with the couple’s child, while they were at the popular destination near the city of Muğla in southwestern Turkey.
Prosecutors told the court that Aysal had taken out a $25,000 accident insurance policy in his wife’s name, making himself the sole beneficiary and collecting the funds immediately after her death.
Aysal – who once attempted to enter a plea of insanity – has maintained his innocence, claiming he never pushed his wife and instead she had disappeared after he turned his back on her for a second.
A witness, who had recorded a video capturing the final moments of Semra Aysal on the cliff, said the husband had appeared “unusually calm” after the incident.
“We even joked, ‘Either this man will throw the woman off or the woman will throw the man.’ There was no interaction between them,'” witness Recep Sahin told police after he shared the footage with them.
Pro-women rights groups were outraged following the court’s decision to release Aysal as they review his appeal.
“The decision is extremely worrying, not only for this case but also in terms of the evaluation of evidence in femicide cases and the debates surrounding impunity,” lawyer Hediye Gökçe Baykal told Cumhuriyet.
The women’s wing of the New Party, Turkey’s social democratic political faction, called for justice for both Semra Aysal and her unborn child.
“A woman and her seven-month-old unborn baby lost their lives. The defendant, who received an aggravated life sentence, is now free,” the party wrote, according to the outlet.
“The Supreme Court has issued a release order for Hakan Aysal, who was sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment for being responsible for the death of his wife, Semra Aysal, in Muğla. We ask: How will accountability be provided for the deaths of Semra and her unborn baby?” the group questioned.

articles.title_zh: Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
articles.content_orig:
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis have said they intercepted two missiles and five drones targeting different parts of the country, allegedly launched by the Iran-backed rebel group.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards Riyadh,” Turki al-Maliki, the Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, said in a post on X early on Sunday.
He said the coalition forces also shot down three drones in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern region on Sunday.
Earlier on Saturday, al-Maliki said two suspected Houthi drones “were intercepted and destroyed” in the Riyadh and southern regions.
Meanwhile, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), claimed to have shot down an armed Saudi coalition reconnaissance aircraft carrying out “hostile operations in the airspace of al-Jawf”.
In a post on X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Iran-aligned group was able to “repel a number of Saudi military formations using several Yemeni-made surface-to-air missiles” and that it was the fifth aircraft the Houthis had shot down since the escalation began.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to the kingdom’s authorities.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, as well as the East-West pipeline and oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia.
The interceptions come as the Saudi-led forces supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government also said they intercepted several drones launched towards the Yemeni city of Marib.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said government forces had made gains against the Houthis during heavy fighting in the al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf, as fighting intensified in Marib.
Al-Nuzaili said 321 Houthi leaders had been killed or wounded in 723 targeted operations by Saudi-backed forces in the Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf governorates, and that 117 military vehicles used by the Iran-allied rebel group had been destroyed.
The coalition carried out at least 37 air strikes and 56 drone attacks, as well as 541 artillery strikes.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the Saudi-led coalition had launched 72 air strikes against the Houthis in the Saada, Taiz, Lahij and al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.
He said the Houthis targeted Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of the Lahij governorate with ballistic missiles.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported that two women and two children were injured as a result of artillery shelling by Saudi-backed forces in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Sanaa, Yemen’s capital controlled by the Houthis.
More than 340,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration.
As the fight between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalated, the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans in the kingdom to exercise “heightened vigilance”, citing an increased threat of Houthi attacks.
The embassy said Houthi attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia had “caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions”, warning that hostilities could spread “rapidly”.
“Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia,” it said.

Two months before Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, it issued a series of far-reaching demands , including that NATO pull its troops back to positions they held in 1997, before the Western alliance expanded toward Russia’s borders.
Now, in closed-door negotiations with President Trump’s envoys this week about how to end the war in Ukraine, the Russians have revived that stance — in some cases word for word — in an effort to attain a larger victory after five years and hundreds of thousands of deaths.
Moscow’s unyielding position was laid out in a paper that Russian officials circulated this week, according to a copy obtained by The New York Times from a person involved in the talks.
The paper, whose authenticity was confirmed by another person with knowledge of the negotiations, shows that President Vladimir V. Putin has scarcely budged on his core objectives after more than 20 months of diplomacy by the Trump administration to end the conflict.
Russia’s demands that NATO pull back forces from its eastern flank in Poland and the Baltics thrust the question of European security into the heart of the negotiations over Ukraine. And they detail the objective behind Mr. Putin’s public statements. The Russian leader has continually insisted that what he calls the “root causes” of the war — Russia’s wide-ranging grievances with both NATO and Ukraine — be addressed before he stops fighting.
The document also underscores how the economic inducements that Mr. Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have offered Mr. Putin have yet to secure concessions from Moscow. To critics, the United States risks enabling Mr. Putin’s long-running attempt to reassert a Soviet-era sphere of influence from Europe to Central Asia.

articles.title_zh: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
articles.content_orig:
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.
In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.
In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.
In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.
It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.
The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

articles.title_orig: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
articles.title_zh: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
articles.content_orig:
An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random.
The United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days. The timing is almost too coincidental to be a coincidence – coming on the heels of the removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO amidst an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, widespread recriminations about chip exports to China, and demands for tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China.
Could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S. infrastructure? It’s too early to know for sure, but the country deserves far more transparent answers than we have received so far.
At 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday , November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every departing flight in America, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the third nationwide ground stop ever ordered. The first came on Sept. 11, 2001; the second more than 20 years later, on Jan. 11, 2023.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would say only that “a communication issue” had struck every one of the 22 centers that guide planes across the country, and that technicians were investigating. A subsequent press conference by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did little to reassure anyone, with no answers about what happened and little reassurance that it would be fixable anytime soon, with airports sending travelers home and communicating that flight cancellations would persist for many hours at a minimum, if not days.
It was the second time in two days that critical infrastructure the country cannot function without simply stopped, potentially for very nefarious reasons. The day before, Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot went dark in 74 countries and stayed down for hours. Both blackouts struck within a day-and-a-half of the most damaging China espionage story in years.
The last nationwide ground stop, in 2023, lasted about 90 minutes and still delayed more than 10,000 flights and canceled 1,300 . Friday’s lasted hours with no resolution imminent on the horizon. At the four-hour point of this latest ground stop, 10,243 flights were already delayed and 3,234 cancelled, with flights grounded not only at single regional airports but across the entire nation, suggesting systemic breakdowns rather than localized issues.
Microsoft’s failure began at 11:17 a.m. ET on Thursday and spread across 19 Microsoft 365 services . Within an hour, complaints about Outlook were running at more than 2,000 times their normal level . Microsoft counts more than 450 million paid commercial seats , with many millions of those users locked out entirely from their inboxes and other critical services.
The casualty list reads like a roll call of essential services: the U.S. House of Representatives was substantively incapacitated; a federal appeals court that could not send or receive email; Britain’s Parliament and its National Health Service, where the failure threatened patients’ prescriptions; Australia’s spy agency and federal police were sent offline as well.
When a botched CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines in 2024, the Fortune 500 alone lost an estimated $5.4 billion . One risk adviser already puts Microsoft’s bill in the billions for Australia alone , not to mention the lost economic value in the U.S. or the rest of the world. This was the first time in history so many users were locked out for so long – with shifting and unsatisfactory explanations. Similarly, this is the first time in global aviation history where there has been a nationwide ground stop with no satisfactory, clear explanation and immediate fix.
Microsoft wrote the playbook for false comfort. For a full day it insisted there was “no indication” of malicious activity while its own bulletins showed it did not know what had broken. If it did not know for sure, then how could they know for sure there was no indication of anything malicious amidst shifting explanations?
First it blamed elevated load, then servers that had unexpectedly dropped out . It found no recent change that lined up with the failure. Hours later, it was rolling back a network change that did . Early Friday, engineers were still trying to “pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx.”
Only on Friday afternoon did Microsoft name a culprit : a flaw introduced during a network capacity upgrade, “not related to cyber.” That sequence is as nonsensical as it is falsely reassuring. No patient would trust a doctor who swears it is not an infection before he can diagnose the fever. You cannot rule out what you cannot yet explain, and nobody can feel particularly reassured from this disturbing sequence of events and shifting explanations.
On Thursday morning, Nvidia, whose board failures we dissected in Fortune this week , announced the resignation of Jensen Huang , the chip industry’s loudest advocate for selling to China, after he admitted an affair with a businesswoman U.S. officials suspect of spying for Beijing . Beijing has been vocal in calling it a smear amidst a rapid escalation of U.S.-China tensions. Lawmakers in both parties are demanding testimony and tighter export controls . Within three hours, inboxes went dark from Capitol Hill to Canberra. A day later, planes stopped and were grounded.
Could that really be a coincidence?
Perhaps we are being too conspiratorial, but there is a certain uncanny resemblance to Beijing’s favorite playbook, which is to divert from negative news stories by shutting down internet services and diverting public attention.
For example, in 2011, a petition to free Ai Weiwei got Change.org knocked offline . In 2012, exposés of the family fortunes of Xi Jinping and Wen Jiabao got Bloomberg and The New York Times blocked in China and targeted by hackers . In 2014, as Hong Kong marched for democracy, a newspaper and a voting site were buried under one of the largest attacks the internet had ever seen . In 2015, China’s “Great Cannon” hammered GitHub for days for hosting banned news. In 2019, Telegram and the LIHKG forum were swamped as Hong Kong marched again. In 2022, news of the zero-COVID protests on Twitter drowned in a deluge of spam . Maybe this pattern of untimely hacks was merely a coincidence – or could it have been more than coincidence?
Microsoft knows this adversary better than anyone. Hackers tied to Beijing tore through its customers’ Exchange servers in 2021 and stole some 60,000 State Department emails through its cloud in 2023, a breach a federal review board blamed on a “cascade of security failures” at Microsoft. Just three weeks ago, Microsoft itself said a China-aligned group had turned AI agents loose on more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 customers .
Whatever the cause, the lesson is identical. Some cyber experts are warning about potentially economically destabilizing cyberattacks, with researchers warning that AI-enabled hacking is spreading like a virus: attacks on previously unknown flaws have roughly doubled since capable open-source models arrived.
U.S. agencies say China’s Volt Typhoon hackers have already burrowed into American communications, transportation, energy and water networks , in some cases for five years, positioning themselves to disrupt them. They sat inside one small Massachusetts electric and water utility for more than 300 days . If the inbox and the skies can go dark on consecutive days, why not the grid, or the tap? Is it time for every business and household to buy storage batteries, water tanks, MREs and porta potties?
Of course, regardless of whether this was a Chinese or foreign malevolent actor attack, or whether it was merely the coincidental degradation of antiquated and outdated infrastructure systems, all of this takes place against the backdrop of the substantive hollowing out of U.S. government cou

articles.title_orig: South Korea’s viral ‘Scarf Man’ tells customers not to buy his products. They’re lining up anyway
articles.title_zh: South Korea’s viral ‘Scarf Man’ tells customers not to buy his products. They’re lining up anyway
articles.content_orig:
Most shopkeepers will do just about anything to make a sale.
But one merchant in Seoul has built an unexpected internet following by doing the exact opposite.
“Didn’t you come here knowing that we sell nothing but crappy stuff?” he asks customers in a video shared on social media. “Didn’t you all come here to buy scarves for your doghouses?”
Meet the Namdaemun Scarf Man.
A merchant in Seoul’s oldest traditional market has become an unlikely internet sensation, with hundreds of people lining up for a chance to hear his brutally honest sales pitch. CNN’s Gage Goulding reports.
His unorthodox sales strategy is the opposite of the hard sell. Instead of talking about how great his products are, he tries to convince shoppers they don’t need a scarf at all. He complains about their requests, pokes fun at their shopping habits and occasionally suggests he might be better off quitting the business altogether.
Maybe it’s reverse psychology. But it’s working.
Hundreds of people have been flocking to his small shop inside Seoul’s sprawling Namdaemun Market for a chance to meet the man behind the viral videos. The international travelers joining the queue may not even be able to understand his Korean-language zingers, but that doesn’t stop them from showing up anyway.
The scarves themselves are hardly a luxury purchase. Six sell for 10,000 won, or about $7. But it seems the merchandise isn’t the point.
Namdaemun is one of Seoul’s most recognizable traditional markets, a  maze of hundreds of shops and stalls. Vendors of clothing, handbags, shoes, household goods and snacks all push up against each other, competing for space. For generations, it has been a place where merchants and customers haggle, bargain and build relationships face-to-face.
Videos of Scarf Man’s colorful exchanges with customers have spread across social media, earning him more than 100,000 Instagram followers and a growing audience on YouTube.
His online popularity has even translated into a new online store, where customers can purchase his scarves without making the trip to Seoul. The first batch of products sold out within 24 hours. Fittingly, Scarf Man has since asked customers to cancel their orders because he received too many.
Still, plenty of fans would rather see the man in person.
Some visitors have traveled considerable distances, only to find his shop closed or the day’s customers already turned away.
Ahn Hyo-sun traveled across Seoul to visit the shop after repeatedly watching clips of Scarf Man online. She arrived hoping to meet him, but missed her chance.
“I heard his voice earlier, so I got really excited thinking he must be here,” she said.
The vendor’s humor provides a welcome pick-me-up. Followers compare his entertaining, occasionally foul-mouthed remarks to those of a hilarious grandmother.
“Listening to this man’s funny banter gives them a kind of happiness boost,” she said.
Another customer, Cho Yoon-sook, traveled roughly an hour and a half from Incheon, west of Seoul, hoping to catch a glimpse of him. She had already been turned away once after arriving too late.
“Maybe I’ll come back tomorrow,” she said. “I’ve made up my mind to come all this way, so I have to see him at least once.”
Cho said she wasn’t particularly interested in the scarves — just in the Scarf Man.
“There’s something endearing about the way he talks,” she said.
For all the attention surrounding him, there’s still plenty about Scarf Man that remains unknown — like his name. In a livestream on social media he shared that he’s married with children and has been selling various products at Namdaemun for years, but that’s about all we know.
Even figuring out when his shop will be open has become something of a guessing game. CNN tried visiting three days in a row this week, and only on the last day did we briefly catch Scarf Man as he closed up his store. As he did so, people watched in awe, with their cameras out, cheering when he turned and gave a quick smile.
These days, it seems like everyone is chasing viral fame, or eager to embrace it if it comes along.
In Italy, Venetian Monica Poli became a social media sensation after she took it upon herself to warn tourists when they were about to be pickpocketed . Poli’s Attenzione, pickpocket! warning became an oft-shared earworm online, and she told CNN that she appreciated being thanked for the work she calls her “mission.”
Meanwhile, a good-looking Istanbul native named Alper Temel became a viral celebrity while selling corn and chestnuts at a roadside stall with his brothers. Online fans dubbed him the “ corn star ” and began flocking to the stall to get selfies. Temel has taken the attention in stride, and the family business is booming.
But Scarf Man doesn’t seem to be chasing the influencer dream.
He has turned down myriad interview requests, including from CNN.
In an age where social media can turn just about anyone into a celebrity, this merchant has found an odd but effective way to stand out: telling people his products aren’t worth buying.
Judging by the lines outside his shop, customers aren’t listening.

articles.title_orig: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to advance peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.
Kushner told reporters on Saturday that “both sides” – Kyiv and Moscow – know that compromises will be necessary to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were now working on the next steps.
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a prisoner exchange .
The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders agreeing on Friday to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not believe it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.
The Kremlin has signalled openness to negotiations with Europe, but has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.
The five countries attending – France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom – have signalled a readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said that the Russian “acceptance, as it has been accepted by Jared Kushner of European participation [in the talks], is something that could actually be important”.
“Kushner makes direct reference as well to the issue of security guarantees required by Ukraine, and he makes clear that it would be NATO that would provide these guarantees,” Hanna said.
Moreover, he added, “as negotiators are suggesting, there might be another round of multilateral negotiations to build on what’s been called ‘substantial progress’ in the recent talks”.
In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said Europe must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.
Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.
Zelenskyy said on Friday that US negotiators had asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas, most of which Russia occupies, in exchange for joining NATO.
The war has raged while negotiations continue. November leaks from Russia’s official statistics agency showed that Moscow’s war effort has so far cost the lives of at least 450,000 soldiers.
